```{r}
#| include: false
s <- readRDS("data/simulations.rds")[["50"]]
usd <- function(x) sprintf("$%.2f", x)
```

Suppose a student wants to estimate average weekly spending on groceries.
They ask 50 people and find that the sample average is close to $50. How much
should they trust that number? A different group of 50 people would probably
give a different average. A confidence interval and a hypothesis test give us
two ways to describe that uncertainty.

I use a simulated example so we can see the truth that real survey data usually
hide. I generate individual spending from a normal distribution with a mean of
$50 and a standard deviation of $10. These values are assumptions for a teaching
example, not actual grocery data. The charts start with 50 people; use the menu
to compare samples of 20 and 100. Each choice shows a separately generated
sample and a fresh set of simulations saved with the post.

```{=html}
<div style="margin:1rem 0"><label for="sample-size">Sample size: <select id="sample-size"><option value="20">20 people</option><option value="50" selected>50 people</option><option value="100">100 people</option></select></label></div>
```

## 1. Build an interval from one sample

First, I draw one sample from the population. To bootstrap it, I draw the same
number of observations from that sample *with replacement*. Some people can
appear more than once in a resample, while others do not appear at all. I
calculate the mean each time and repeat this process 500 times. The middle 95%
of those bootstrap means, between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, gives a
percentile bootstrap interval.

```{=html}
<div id="bootstrap-chart" style="width:100%;min-height:360px" aria-label="Histogram of bootstrap sample means"></div>
<p id="bootstrap-note"></p>
```

For the sample of 50, the mean is `r usd(s$sample_mean)`, and the interval runs
from `r usd(s$interval[1])` to `r usd(s$interval[2])`. The histogram shows how
the mean changes when we reuse the observed sample. The interval is not a
range containing 95% of individual grocery bills; it describes uncertainty
about the population mean.

## 2. Repeat the whole exercise

One interval cannot tell us whether the procedure works in the long run. Here I
draw 1,000 independent samples from the population and construct a new bootstrap
interval for each one. The chart displays the first 100 intervals. A teal line
contains the true mean of $50; an orange line misses it. The count below the
chart uses all 1,000 intervals, including those not shown.

```{=html}
<div id="coverage-chart" style="width:100%;min-height:440px" aria-label="Bootstrap confidence intervals across repeated samples"></div>
<p id="coverage-note"></p>
```

With 50 people, `r s$covered_count` of the 1,000 intervals contain $50:
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100*s$coverage)`%. That is close to 95%, although it need
not equal exactly 95% in a finite simulation. With 20 people, the same run
covers $50 in `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*readRDS("data/simulations.rds")[["20"]]$coverage)`% of intervals. Simulation noise and the percentile method's
finite-sample accuracy can both contribute to the difference. A 95% confidence level describes
the performance of the procedure across repeated samples. Once we compute one
interval, it either contains the fixed population mean or it does not; it is
not correct to assign that particular fixed interval a 95% probability of
containing the fixed mean.

## 3. Test a $50 mean

Now consider a different question: would the observed sample mean be unusual
if the population mean really were $50? My null hypothesis is that the mean
is $50. For this teaching example, I also assume the population distribution is
normal with a known $10 standard deviation. I simulate 5,000 new sample means
under those assumptions. The orange tails mark the most extreme 5% of the
simulated absolute deviations from $50, split between the two sides.

```{=html}
<div id="null-chart" style="width:100%;min-height:360px" aria-label="Null distribution of sample means and rejection region"></div>
<p id="null-note"></p>
<noscript>These charts require JavaScript. The R simulation code and saved results are linked below.</noscript>
<script src="vendor/plotly-basic-2.35.2.min.js"></script>
<script src="data/simulations.js"></script>
<script src="code/charts.js"></script>
```

The solid line shows the observed sample mean. I calculate a two-sided p-value
as the fraction of null simulations at least as far from $50 as that mean. For
50 people, it is about `r sprintf("%.3f", s$p_value)`, so this example does not
reject the null at the 5% level. A p-value is not the probability that the null
hypothesis is true. It measures how unusual the sample result would be under
the stated null model. Both the simulated cutoff and p-value have some Monte
Carlo variation; a different random seed can change them slightly.

## Takeaway

The bootstrap uses one sample to estimate uncertainty, while repeated sampling
lets us check how often the interval procedure covers a known truth. A hypothesis
test asks a related but different question: how unusual is the observed result
under a particular null model? Try changing the sample size and compare the
widths and p-values. The sample changes too, so the p-value need not move in
one direction. The near-95% coverage here depends on this simulation setup and
does not guarantee the same coverage for every population or bootstrap method.

## Reproduce the simulation

The [R script](code/simulate.R) records the random seed, 500 bootstrap
resamples per interval, 1,000 coverage samples, and 5,000 null simulations.
The [chart code](code/charts.js), [saved results](data/simulations.rds), and
[README](README.md) explain how to rerun the example. The Plotly library is
included locally, so the interactive charts do not require a live data service.
